{{Short description|Property of integer sequences}}

In [[mathematics]], '''Gauss congruence''' is a property held by certain [[sequence]]s of [[integer]]s, including the [[Lucas numbers]] and the [[divisor function|divisor sum]] sequence. Sequences satisfying this property are also known as Dold sequences, Fermat sequences, Newton sequences, and realizable sequences.<ref name="dold">{{cite journal |last1=Byszewski |first1=Jakub |last2=Graff |first2=Grzegorz |last3=Ward |first3=Thomas |title=Dold sequences, periodic points, and dynamics |journal=Bull. Lond. Math. Soc. |date=2021 |volume=53 |issue=5 |pages=1263–1298|doi=10.1112/blms.12531 |arxiv=2007.04031 }}</ref> The property is named after [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] (1777–1855), although Gauss never defined the property explicitly.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Smyth |first1=Chris |title=A coloring proof of a generalisation of Fermat's little theorem |journal=American Mathematical Monthly |date=1986 |volume=93 |issue=6 |pages=469–471|doi=10.1080/00029890.1986.11971858 }}</ref>

Sequences satisfying Gauss congruence naturally occur in the study of [[topological dynamics]], [[algebraic number theory]] and [[combinatorics]].<ref name="trace">{{cite journal |last1=Zarelua |first1=A. V. |title=On congruences for the traces of powers of some matrices |journal=Tr. Mat. Inst. Steklova |date=2008 |volume=263 |pages=85–105}}</ref>

== Definition ==

A sequence of integers <math>(a_1,a_2,\dots)</math> satisfies Gauss congruence if
: <math>\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)a_{n/d}\equiv 0\pmod{n}</math>
for every <math>n\geq 1</math>, where <math>\mu</math> is the [[Möbius function]]. By [[Möbius inversion formula|Möbius inversion]], this condition is equivalent to the existence of a sequence of integers <math>(b_1,b_2,\dots)</math> such that
: <math>a_n=\sum_{d\mid n}b_dd</math>
for every <math>n\geq 1</math>. Furthermore, this is equivalent to the existence of a sequence of integers <math>(c_1,c_2,\dots)</math> such that
: <math>a_n=c_1a_{n-1}+c_2a_{n-2}+\cdots+c_{n-1}a_1+nc_n</math>
for every <math>n\geq 1</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Du |first1=Bau-Sen |last2=Huang |first2=Sen-Shan |last3=Li |first3=Ming-Chia |title=Newton, Fermat and exactly realizable sequences |journal=J. Integer Seq. |date=2005 |volume=8 |pages=Article 05.1.2|bibcode=2005JIntS...8...12D }}</ref> If the values <math>c_n</math> are eventually zero, then the sequence <math>(a_1,a_2,\dots)</math> satisfies a [[linear recurrence]].

A direct relationship between the sequences <math>(b_1,b_2,\dots)</math> and <math>(c_1,c_2,\dots)</math> is given by the equality of [[generating function]]s
: <math>\sum_{n\geq 1}c_nx^n=1-\prod_{n\geq 1}(1-x^n)^{b_n}</math>.

== Examples ==

Below are examples of sequences <math>(a_n)_{n\geq 1}</math> known to satisfy Gauss congruence.

* <math>(a^n)</math> for any integer <math>a</math>, with <math>c_1=a</math> and <math>c_n=0</math> for <math>n>1</math>.
* <math>{\rm{tr}}(A^n)</math> for any [[Matrix (mathematics)#Square matrix|square matrix]] <math>A</math> with integer entries.<ref name="trace" />
* The divisor-sum sequence <math>(1,3,4,7,6,12,\dots)</math>, with <math>b_n=1</math> for every <math>n\geq 1</math>.
* The Lucas numbers <math>(1,3,4,7,11,18\dots)</math>, with <math>c_1=c_2=1</math> and <math>c_n=0</math> for every <math>n>2</math>.

== In dynamical systems ==

Consider a discrete-time [[dynamical system]], consisting of a set <math>X</math> and a map <math>T:X\to X</math>. We write <math>T^n</math> for the <math>n</math><sup>th</sup> iteration of the map, and say an element <math>x</math> in <math>X</math> has ''period'' <math>n</math> if <math>T^nx=x</math>.

Suppose the number of points in <math>X</math> with period <math>n</math> is finite for every <math>n\geq 1</math>. If <math>a_n</math> denotes the number of such points, then the sequence <math>(a_n)_{n\geq 1}</math> satisfies Gauss congruence, and the associated sequence <math>(b_n)_{n\geq 1}</math> counts orbits of size <math>n</math>.<ref name="dold" />

For example, fix a positive integer <math>\alpha</math>. If <math>X</math> is the set of [[Necklace (combinatorics)#Aperiodic necklaces|aperiodic necklaces]] with beads of <math>\alpha</math> colors and <math>T</math> acts by rotating each necklace clockwise by a bead, then <math>a_n=\alpha^n</math> and <math>b_n</math> counts [[Lyndon word]]s of length <math>n</math> in an alphabet of <math>\alpha</math> letters.

== In algebraic number theory ==

Gauss congruence can be extended to sequences of [[rational]] numbers, where such a sequence <math>(a_n)_{n\geq 1}</math> satisfies Gauss congruence ''at a prime'' <math>p</math> if
: <math>\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)a_{n/d}\equiv 0\pmod{n}</math>
for every <math>n=p^r</math> with <math>r\geq 1</math>, or equivalently, if <math>a_{p^r}\equiv a_{p^{r-1}}\text{ mod }p^r</math> for every <math>r\geq 1</math>.

A sequence of rational numbers <math>(a_n)_{n\geq 1}</math> defined by a linear recurrence satisfies Gauss congruence at all but finitely many primes if and only if
: <math>a_n=\sum_{i=1}^r q_i{\mathrm{Tr}}_{\mathbb{K}\mid\mathbb{Q}}(\theta_i^n)</math>,
where <math>\mathbb{K}</math> is an [[algebraic number field]] with <math>\theta_1,\dots,\theta_r\in\mathbb{K}</math>, and <math>q_1,\dots,q_r\in\mathbb{Q}</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Minton |first1=Gregory |title=Linear recurrence sequences satisfying congruence conditions |journal=Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. |date=2014 |volume=142 |issue=7 |pages=2337–2352|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-2014-12168-X |doi-access=free }}</ref>
